items._ogDesc: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the meeting with Stellantis officials was “challenging” but “productive.”
items.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the meeting with Stellantis officials was “challenging” but “productive.”

“We’re just going to keep fighting. We were very clear. We don’t want that facility to be closed or sold,” Ford told reporters after he left the meeting with Stellantis, which was also attended by Federal Industry Minister Melanie Joly and Unifor National President Lana Payne.

“We want production there, so we want to focus on Brampton. Want to make sure they maintain the people in Windsor as well.”

Ahead of the meeting, four sources briefed on the confidential talks told CTV News that there was little optimism that the federal government could stop the sale of the Brampton Assembly plant to Roshel.

“We had a very, I think, frank discussion,” Payne told reporters when asked how the meeting went.

She said while the automaker was “unwavering” that the sale would close, Stellantis agreed to continue to have dialogue next week. Payne confirmed that the COO of Stellantis North America will be visiting Canada.

“I still think we have a very big mountain to climb here,” Payne said. “I don’t want to sugarcoat this. We’re up against it.”

items._ogDesc: Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle in Newfoundland and Labrador.
items.body:
ST. JOHN’S — Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project has cleared its final regulatory hurdle in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Officials with the federal and provincial governments announced today they had accepted the development’s approval by the Canada-Newfoundland and Labrador Offshore Energy Regulator.

Premier Tony Wakeham says the approval was an important milestone ahead of Equinor’s final decision next year on whether it will proceed with the project.

He said his government is still considering whether to buy a 10 per cent stake in the $14-billion development.

Bay du Nord would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada, and farther from shore than any other oil project on Earth.

Norway-based Equinor would drill wells more than a kilometre below the surface of the ocean, in waters about 500 kilometres northeast of St. John’s, N.L.

The company expects to extract more than 400 million barrels of oil, with first oil expected in 2031.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

items._ogDesc: .S. President Donald Trump said Canada is feeling “emboldened” but his administration is working on a trade deal “that’s fair” in a wide-ranging news conference at the White House on Friday.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday Canada is feeling “emboldened” but his administration is working on a trade deal “that’s fair.”

In a wide-ranging news conference at the White House, the president said he spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, and described the Canadian leader as “very nice.”

Trump then turned to his repeated claims about Canada ripping off the United States and being frustrating to deal with on the trade file.

“For some reason they feel emboldened and we can’t let them feel that way anymore,” Trump said.

It wasn’t clear exactly what the president was referring to — the historically close Canada-U.S. relationship or the midterm elections which saw American voters issue a clear rebuke of Trump’s trade policy and sweeping tariff campaign.

Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. The president hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others, prompting Ottawa to respond with retaliatory duties.

Trump also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and spent days posting images on social media disparaging Canada.

The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after the Republican shellacking in the midterm elections.

On Nov. 12, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said “we want to have a deal that makes sense for them and for us.”

“Part of it means protecting our supply chains and getting them here, but also making accommodation when possible,” Greer said.

Trump said Friday that when Canada’s trade deficit with the United States is down to zero, he’ll be ready to talk. That trade deficit is driven by U.S. consumption of oil and energy products, which Trump also has said he wants to increase.

The president repeated Friday the claim that Carney wants to “build a Keystone pipeline for us” — likely a reference to the Prairie Connector pipeline that would reuse Keystone XL infrastructure.

Carney on Wednesday said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait. Carney has embarked on a mission to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States, including signing trade deals last week with the Philippines and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations group.

“We’d like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn’t want to do a deal, we’re busy,” Carney said in an interview during the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Canada’s Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette has said Canada must prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement may no longer be possible.

The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette told MPs during a meeting Tuesday of the House of Commons international trade committee in Ottawa.

Democrats have indicated ending the trade war with Canada will be among their top priorities when they take control of Congress in January — but they could struggle to achieve the supermajority they need to override the president’s veto.

Canada will also need to continue working with the Trump administration to renew the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as CUSMA.

Trump did not renew CUSMA in July, triggering a rolling annual review for up to a decade — at which point the agreement will expire if the three countries cannot agree on an extension.

During Friday’s nearly 90-minute press briefing where Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the president also said companies that build artificial intelligence data centres in other countries will be hit with “a tremendous tax.”

“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen,” Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

Trump said he hadn’t yet told his own officials about his plan and offered no details. Throughout the president’s second term he has suggested tariffs and punishments for a wide range of actions that have never materialized.

Unease over the fast pace of data centre development in the U.S. also helped Democrats win big in the midterm elections.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

items.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
items.description: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10 per cent from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3 per cent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9 per cent.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1 per cent.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5 per cent overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at both the federal and state level.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.”

Much of the AI rout was centreed among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centres. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 per cent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 per cent and Broadcom fell 12.1 per cent. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7 per cent.

Corning slid 10.9 per cent and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3 per cent.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8 per cent lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25 per cent.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1 per cent to US$88.30, but remains above its IPO price of US$83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing US$2 trillion in value.

Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23 per cent decline from its brief peak of US$115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 per cent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7 per cent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 per cent.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.04 per cent late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6 per cent to settle at US$92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

items.title: 'Most ambitious since Avro': Ottawa defence startup unveils partners for Scout drone
items.description: Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry’s leading contractors around the world: We’re coming for your lunch.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Dominion Dynamics founder Eliot Pence speaks at the 2026 Toronto Tech Week Homecoming conference in Toronto, on Wednesday, May 27, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sammy Kogan]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Sammy Kogan</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry’s leading contractors around the world: We’re coming for your lunch.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Eliot Pence, the hard-charging founder of Canadian defence company Dominion Dynamics, has a message for the industry’s leading contractors around the world: We’re coming for your lunch.

The fledgling Ottawa-based startup unveiled twelve partnerships with established defence players in Canada on Friday for developing its Scout drone, an uncrewed “loyal wingman” reliant on artificial intelligence that could pair with fighter jets and fly alongside them.

Dominion is planning to compete in an anticipated future procurement to supply the federal government with autonomous collaborative platforms. It’s bringing a made-in-Canada pitch to the competition at a time when Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is focused on acquiring sovereign capabilities and building up domestic industries.

“The intention here is for it to be the most ambitious air platform since the Avro in Canada,” Pence told The Canadian Press.

Avro Canada was a post-Second World War aerospace manufacturer known mainly for its CF-105 Arrow, a highly regarded but short-lived interceptor jet.

Dominion’s project has been in the works since his company’s inception some 18 months ago. Pence is quickly assembling plans for a supply chain that would be mostly domestic.

Dominion’s early development partners include Pratt and Whitney Canada -- it plans to use PW300-type engines in its drones -- Telesat, Top Aces, North Aircraft Industries, PV Labs, SRC Can, Thales Canada and Altitude Aerospace.

Pence’s company would build the drone and its systems for handling data communication, sensors and intelligence, and turn to these other companies for expertise in areas such as operator training, avionics and landing gear.

Dominion also announced a stand-alone partnership with Canadian satellite operator Telesat this week to make antennas designed for Arctic use. They would connect uncrewed military hardware systems to Lightspeed, Telesat’s planned low-Earth satellite network.

The federal government awarded a $17 million contract to Dominion Dynamics this week. The 24-month contract was awarded to the company to build a remotely controlled marine drone that can survey the ocean floor to detect, locate and identify underwater mines.

The federal government’s website said the drone will allow the Royal Canadian Navy to conduct missions by providing near real-time transmission of data while keeping personnel and crewed vessels outside of threat areas.

With Canada’s current CF-18 Hornet fighter jets expected to reach the end of their service lives by 2032, Ottawa has started acquiring advanced F-35 stealth fighters made by Lockheed Martin, although the jets are not yet based in Canada.

Shortly after taking office in early 2025, Carney’s government launched a review of Ottawa’s plan to purchase a fleet of 88 F-35s.

Saab, the Swedish defence manufacturer that was a runner-up in Canada’s fighter jet competition, has said it could set up a manufacturing hub in Canada for its Gripen fighter jets if Ottawa chooses to put in a bulk order for those aircraft.

Pence said Dominion’s drones would work with either the F-35 or the Gripen, and with other platforms like the early warning and control aircraft Canada wants to acquire.

These companies and other large legacy defence firms are developing similar kinds of drones they can sell alongside their crewed platforms.

Pence said he believes all of these companies are at the same starting line, since the technology is so new. And he’s betting that offering a Canadian-made drone designed for the vast and harsh Arctic environment gives his company an edge.

“We are building for the specific Arctic problem set and nobody else is doing that,” he said.

“There are very specific problems we’re seeking to solve for the RCAF -- range, Arctic ruggedization, gravel runway takeoff, short runways.”

Pence said he expects the government will launch a procurement competition for autonomous platforms in 2028 or 2029.

He said he intends to have the Dominion Scout flying in late 2028.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

items.title: Trump administration use of encrypted messaging apps like Signal is scrutinized by House Democrat
items.description: A top U.S. House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[An FBI seal is displayed on a podium before a news conference at the field office in Portland, Ore., Jan. 16, 2025. (AP Photo/Jenny Kane)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jenny Kane</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A top U.S. House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.

Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the U.S. Justice Department, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the U.S. Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.

But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s general counsel and an associate of the Republican president’s oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potential or ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.

The U.S. Justice Department said in a statement Friday that it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.” The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said it complies with all applicable federal laws, including those governing the retention of documents.

Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.

Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.

Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.

The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

By Eric Tucker, The Associated Press

items.title: Claude may have cracked mathematics’ greatest unsolved riddle
items.description: A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm’s Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.

items._ogDesc: A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm’s Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.
items.body:
WASHINGTON -- A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm’s Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpoge wrote in a four-page note released Friday.

The claim has not been independently verified, and the proof has not yet been reviewed by outside experts.

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is widely regarded as the most important open question in pure mathematics.

It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, which offers $1 million for a solution to each.

Under the institute’s rules, a solution must be published in a peer-reviewed journal and withstand two years of scrutiny.

Alpoge said the method also resolves a broader version of the problem known as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.

He said he and Claude had produced a version of the proof in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical arguments to be checked by computer, and that he was releasing only that version for now.

A full written argument would be extremely long, he said, adding that he had not yet mastered all of the mathematics involved and planned to write it up properly.

Alpoge said he had consulted Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei before announcing the result, and acknowledged that its timing could be viewed cynically, without elaborating, though he was probably referring to this week’s record IPO.

In August, Anthropic said an unreleased version of Claude had improved a long-standing result related to the Riemann Hypothesis, while stressing that it had not proved it.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment from AFP.

The claim comes two months after rival OpenAI said an AI model had solved another Millennium Prize Problem, on the equations that govern how fluids move.

Mathematicians say that proof appears correct but has yet to be fully vetted.

Alpoge, who had worked on related fluid problems with New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, was at the centre of a dispute over credit for that work. OpenAI denied wrongdoing.

items.description: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.content: <p>Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639307993355301439.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.body:
With the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) just around the corner, BMO BrokerEdge is doubling down on its support for the mortgage broker community as a sponsor of the industry-renowned awards ceremony, now entering its landmark 20th year.

Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the bank was putting its weight behind the CMAs – which take place at Rebel Toronto on Wednesday (November 25) – because of its commitment to a flourishing mortgage broker sector as the housing and mortgage markets continue to evolve.

“BMO BrokerEdge is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards in celebrating the professionals and organizations making an impact across the broker community,” she said. “Recognizing industry excellence and fostering strong partnerships are at the heart of our commitment to supporting a thriving mortgage broker landscape across Canada.”

Excellence Awardees are up for prizes across a range of shortlisted categories at the event, with awards recognizing the leading brokers, lenders, service providers, and more.

Other awards up for grabs include the Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing an individual who has made an outstanding contribution to the sector over a lengthy career.

Doolittle said honouring the industry’s top performers benefits the wider mortgage space. “Recognizing excellence shines a light on the professionals and organizations driving meaningful progress across the sector,” she said.

“Their commitment to innovation, client service, and collaboration strengthens the broker channel and leads to better outcomes for Canadian homebuyers.”

The CMAs draw nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and service providers from coast to coast.

A significant year for BrokerEdge

With 2026 winding to a close, Doolittle said the year has been an important one for BMO’s mortgage broker relationships. “2026 has been a milestone year for BMO BrokerEdge, marked by our national expansion and ongoing investment in the broker channel,” she said.

“As more Canadians choose to work with mortgage brokers, we remain focused on improving our service, processes, and programs to help brokers meet their clients’ evolving needs.”

Doolittle said a key priority for the company this year has been improving the day-to-day experience for brokers and their clients by enhancing the overall experience and continuing to improve products, processes, and digital capabilities.

She singled out the lender’s rate guarantee as one way BrokerEdge aims to stand out. “We will continue to differentiate our offering with features such as our 130-day rate guarantee, providing greater flexibility and confidence to homebuyers,” she said.

The company has also rolled out process changes through the year. “We’ve implemented process enhancements, helping create a more seamless and efficient experience,” Doolittle said. “This reflects our ongoing commitment to make it easier for brokers to do business with BMO BrokerEdge and deliver strong outcomes for their clients.”

Looking ahead to 2027

In the year ahead, BMO BrokerEdge intends to keep investing in the broker channel – including resources and support to help brokers grow their business and serve their clients, according to Doolittle.

She said the broker community was an essential part of the big steps taken by the company in recent times. “We would like to thank our broker partners across Canada for their continued trust, collaboration, and support throughout the year,” she said.

“The success of our channel is built on strong relationships, a shared commitment to clients, and a collective focus on raising the bar for our industry.”

Nobody has a crystal ball when it comes to what’s in store for 2027, but Doolittle said she’s optimistic about what’s around the corner for the mortgage industry and market. “As we look toward 2027, we’re optimistic about the opportunities ahead and remain committed to investing in the broker channel, investing in our capabilities, and helping our partners deliver exceptional outcomes for Canadian homebuyers,” she said.

items.description: As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more
items.content: <p>As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307927281564307.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) mark their 20th anniversary on November 25 at Rebel Toronto – and the private lending category has never been more hotly contested.

With private mortgage originations in Ontario reaching $32 billion in 2024, up from $11 billion a decade earlier according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award has become one of the ceremony's most closely watched honours.

For Joe Flor, vice-president of national sales and broker relations at CMI Financial Group in Toronto, which sponsors the award, the recognition carries real industry weight.

Private mortgage lending in Ontario accounted for 15.8% of all mortgage originations in 2024, according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA)'s annual Private Residential Mortgage Lending Report, released in August 2025.

While that figure represents a slight contraction from prior years, the decade-long trend has moved sharply upward – from $11 billion in privately funded mortgages in Ontario in 2015 to $32 billion in 2024, per FSRA data.

For CMI, which sponsored the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award at the 2026 CMAs, the event is more than a celebration.

"I think it's important for us to recognize lenders and brokers that excel in their profession and in their trade," Flor told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It sets the standards for all those that are coming into the industry and also for other lenders who are trying to improve their broker experience."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Canadian Mortgages Inc. in recognizing excellence with the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/hrh5z64Cj6 https://t.co/j3G74SCkSy — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 16, 2026

Knowing the lender matters as much as knowing the product

Flor pointed to a persistent gap he sees in how some brokers approach private files – one that grows more consequential as more Canadians turn to private channels due to qualification challenges, elevated debt-to-income ratios, and credit blemishes that prevent them from accessing traditional lending.

"It's important to understand the specialized solutions available," he said.

"It's also important to understand the lender that you're partnering with because there are a lot of private lenders and it's kind of overwhelming when you're trying to figure out which lender to partner with."

The importance of due diligence on the lender side is not purely a commercial concern.

FSRA's consumer research found that the mortgage delinquency rate among non-bank lenders rose to 0.20 per cent in the third quarter of 2024, up from 0.14 per cent in the same quarter of 2022, according to Statistics Canada. The regulator has identified insufficient exit strategies as one of the key risks for private borrowers, and has maintained private mortgage brokering as a supervisory priority in both its 2024–25 and 2025–26 supervision plans.

For Flor, that underscores a responsibility brokers carry when placing clients in private products.

"Credibility goes a long way," he said.

"You want to know you're putting your client in the right solution with the right lender and not compromising them, potentially in a year or two down the road."

The 2026 excellence awardees for the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending include Cheryl Pienta of FC Funding, David Clarke of TMG The Mortgage Group, Davinder Powar of AKAL Mortgages Inc., and Geoff Lee of GLM Mortgage Group.

CMI Signature and a push toward one-stop-shop lending

Ahead of the ceremony, CMI has been moving on a product expansion it hopes will deepen its value to the broker channel. The lender launched its CMI Signature product in Ontario this week – a new offering aimed at broadening its reach beyond its core private lending mandate.

Flor described a second product launch slated for the following week, which he characterised as an alt-minus solution, alongside several additional products targeted for release in early to mid-2027, subject to third-party approvals.

The broader ambition, he said, is to become a one-stop-shop lender capable of offering a graduation program – a pathway that would allow clients who enter CMI as private borrowers to transition through the lending spectrum into more conventional products as their financial profiles improve.

"CMI is really focused on the broker experience, the customer experience, and providing those solutions and also ensuring that the ease of that transaction is there," he said.

"A lot of digitisation, a lot of technology is being poured into it, and we want to be one of the leaders in the industry of driving that technology aspect of it."

items.description: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.content: <p>Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_639307939243156766.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.body:
Most brokers have tried AI tools to draft emails and answer quick questions. What they haven't had is an AI assistant that knows their deals and can work on them.

Lendesk built Sidekick to close that gap. Sidekick launched in open beta at Finmo Momentum 2026 on November 24 and it's a new AI assistant inside Finmo, Lendesk's mortgage origination platform. It runs in a chat panel next to the broker's deals, where it reads the application and documents, makes updates on request, and looks up lender rates and guidelines. The broker never has to leave the deal.

“We wanted to give brokers a tool that actually works the deal, instead of just surfacing information about it. Sidekick knows the deal, knows the lenders, and takes on the admin, so brokers can spend more time with clients,” said Carter Zimmerman, president of Lendesk.

From single tasks to the whole deal

Each of Finmo's earlier AI tools did one job. In 2024, Finmo added AI deal create, which builds a new application from an email chain, call transcript or notes, and AI fill from document, which pulls property details from an MLS listing into the deal. This year Finmo added AI down payment verification and income verification, which cut hours of document review down to minutes.

Sidekick works differently. It doesn't run one fixed process. It can help with any task a broker does in Finmo: building and editing deals, managing documents, running down payment and income verification, calculating GDS/TDS, and researching lenders.

“Our first AI tools each solved one problem well. Sidekick ties them together,” Zimmerman said. “For the first time, a broker can ask for help the way they’d ask a colleague and get it across the whole deal.”

Ask Sidekick to organize and review a deal’s documents, and it renames files consistently, moves them into the right document conditions, and adds any missing conditions. It then runs down payment and income verification.

Ask Sidekick which rental income approach works best for a conventional deal, and it compares lenders’ add-back and offset policies using Lender Spotlight. It estimates the impact on GDS/TDS and compares available rates and requirements, helping identify the best fit and the lowest-rate option that meets the lender’s stated qualifying limits.

“Sidekick takes what you thought was a B deal and turns it into an A deal,” said Joe Tomkins, Director of User Development & Enablement at Lendesk.

Placing the deal

Sidekick connects to Lender Spotlight, so it can match a deal against lender policies and pull current rates. The "Place this deal" flow works the deal the way an experienced broker would. It grades the deal, screens lenders on their guidelines, and compares rates. Then it gives one recommendation, with a short list of alternatives.

“Finding the right lender for a deal takes experience, plus a lot of checking rates and guidelines across dozens of lenders,” Zimmerman said. “Sidekick handles the checking in one request, so brokers get to the right shortlist faster.”

The broker makes the call

By default, Sidekick asks before it changes anything. Each update, whether it's an edit to the application or a credit pull, shows up as an approval card with the exact change. Nothing is saved until the broker approves it. Read-only tasks, like reviewing the deal or running GDS/TDS numbers, happen right away.

Sidekick also works within the broker's own permissions, so it can only see and do what that broker already can in Finmo — and brokers can delete their chat history at any time.

“In mortgages, trust isn't optional,” Zimmerman said. “That's why Sidekick shows every change before it's made. The broker is always in control.”

Sidekick is available now in open beta, free while the beta runs. Brokers already on Finmo can ask their team admin to turn it on through Finmo support. Brokers new to Finmo can sign up and request access when they join.

items.title: Most Canadians are planning retirement without their biggest asset
items.description: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.content: <p>Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307922816363281.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.body:
Two-thirds of Canadian homeowners rank their property as their single largest financial asset, yet only 27% consider that housing wealth a resource for retirement, according to new research from HomeEquity Bank and Ipsos.

The contrast with registered savings instruments is stark. Sixty-six percent of homeowners rank their property as their primary financial asset. Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) or Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs) come a distant second at 8%, followed by workplace pensions at 6% and Tax-Free Savings Accounts (TFSAs) at 4%.

However, only 27% consider home equity a viable resource in Canadian retirement planning. The home is treated as wealth, not income.

The gap between asset and cash flow

Among survey respondents, 41% feel financially secure but worry about having enough readily available cash, while 40% are not confident they could absorb a major unexpected expense without significantly changing their lifestyle.

Retiring with mortgage debt is fast becoming the norm for Canadians, adding a further layer of pressure. Among those approaching retirement, 35% have delayed their planned retirement date and 49% expect to work part-time.

Among retirees, 29% are spending more monthly than anticipated, with 28% drawing more heavily on investments than planned.

“Canadians have done something incredibly important over their working lives: they’ve built wealth,” said Pattie Lovett-Reid, chief financial commentator at HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, Ontario.

“Retirement planning isn’t just about accumulating assets. It’s about having the right combination of assets, income and cash flow throughout retirement.”

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

A growing opportunity for brokers

Pierre Martin, senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in August that the reverse mortgage conversation is increasingly central for brokers working with existing clients.

“Segment your database. Reconnect with clients aged 55 and older. Ask better questions about retirement and family goals, and know when to bring home equity back into the conversation,” he said.

Rene Quercia, also senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, reinforced that message in a February event.

“In many cases, older folks are retiring with mortgages or with debt and interest rates on that debt are going up, not down. So I think many brokers, when they’re faced with these types of clients now, see reverse mortgages as a good option to present to clients,” he said.

Yvonne Ziomecki-Fisher, chief customer, brand and advice officer at HomeEquity Bank, said home equity deserves inclusion in every retirement planning discussion. 

“Home equity won’t be the right choice for everyone, but it deserves a place in the retirement planning conversation. For some homeowners, it can provide greater flexibility, strengthen cash flow and help manage unexpected expenses while allowing them to continue living in the home they love,” she said.

The Ipsos survey was fielded October 26–27, among 1,500 Canadians aged 18 and older.

items.title: Bank of Canada warns against excessive reliance on rate signals
items.description: Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals
items.content: <p>Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307886080356256.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is urging financial markets to exercise independent judgment on the rate outlook rather than simply reflect the central bank’s own signals.

Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle, speaking before the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce in Edmonton, Alberta, on November 18, warned that too much forward guidance — public signalling of where the overnight rate may head next — risks eroding the independent analysis markets must apply.

The speech follows the Bank’s decision to raise its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.50% at its October 28 announcement, its first hike in more than three years. The final rate announcement of the year set for December 9.

“In a sense, they stop doing their homework,” Gravelle said. “As a result, central banks can lose an important source of information about how investors view the economy.”

The comments echo warnings issued by Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the United States Federal Reserve, who argued in August that forward guidance risks locking policymakers into future decisions.

When scenarios replace explicit guidance

Rather than committing to a rate path, Gravelle said the Bank of Canada has leaned more heavily on scenario analysis — alternative economic projections that show how monetary policy might react if key risks materialize.

A scenario published in the April Monetary Policy Report (MPR) assumed oil prices, then near US$100 per barrel, would ease to roughly US$75 per barrel by mid-2027.

By October, the actual path had tracked the more adverse outcome.

“In the April high oil price scenario, inflation stays close to 3% for more than a year, and consecutive policy rate increases are needed to get inflation back to target,” Gravelle said. That scenario, he noted, had by October largely materialized.

Canada's annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, strengthening expectations that the Bank of Canada may pause at its December 9 rate decision as markets assess easing price pressures and softer economic data. https://t.co/jzZrTP5pgU — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 17, 2026

What higher rates mean for brokers

According to the Bank of Canada’s Q3 Market Participants Survey, financial market participants revised their five-year Government of Canada bond yield} forecasts upward by 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.50%, with the consensus terminal policy rate settling at 2.75%.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Canada, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in September that clients should not wait on pre-approvals.

“So it is a time when we should encourage anyone that is interested in potentially buying a home that they get pre-approved, because today’s rates, even though they’re a little above what they were last week and the week before, they’re only going higher,” she said.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, Ontario, said the October rate hike was designed to buy time.

“We think this hike buys the Bank a few months to assess whether higher energy and input costs are actually filtering through to consumer prices,” he said, projecting one further 25-basis-point increase in Q1 2027.

items.title: Montreal fintech nesto names SVP to accelerate operational growth
items.body:
nesto group(e), the Montreal-based mortgage technology and lending platform, has appointed Louis-François Poirier as Senior Vice President, Strategic Operations. The company says the hire will accelerate execution and unlock new opportunities across its fast-growing Canadian lending business.

Poirier reports to Damien Charbonneau, Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer of nesto group(e).

A veteran operator joins a fast-moving platform

Poirier arrives with more than two decades of senior leadership across two of Canada’s most prominent financial institutions.

He spent 17 years at National Bank of Canada in Montreal, advancing from credit risk analyst through mortgage product management, credit card products, and customer strategy.

From 2020 to 2025, he held a succession of vice-presidential roles at Desjardins — culminating as VP of Retail Lending, Everyday Banking and Savings Products — where he led five business lines with direct profit-and-loss accountability and oversaw two major technology transformation programmes: a loan origination system overhaul and a core banking platform migration.

Most recently, he ran LFP Conseil, an advisory firm he established in January, where he partnered with executive teams on portfolio performance, credit strategy, and operating model scalability before joining nesto group(e).

“After 20+ years in financial services, I’m drawn to nesto’s ambition to reshape Canadian lending,” Poirier wrote in a LinkedIn post.

“I can’t wait to roll up my sleeves with the team and scale our business.”

His appointment follows a period of significant momentum. The company closed a C$302-million Series E financing round in June at a C$1.47-billion valuation, now administers more than C$80 billion in mortgages, and reported over C$37 billion in originations through 2026 alone.

In October, Deloitte ranked nesto #9 on its Technology Fast 50 list, recognising 3,311% revenue growth over three years.

Building the lending ecosystem of the future

Founded in 2018 by Malik Yacoubi, Charbonneau, Karim Benabdallah, and Chase Belair, nesto group(e) operates across the nesto, CMLS, and Intellifi brands and licenses its Nesto Cloud platform to partners including IG Wealth Management, Equitable Bank, and Canada Life.

Its June 2024 acquisition of CMLS Group — formerly Canada’s third-largest independent mortgage finance company, with more than 50 years of operating history — extended the platform into commercial origination, asset management, institutional servicing, and software licensing across all Canadian jurisdictions.

The company employs more than 1,000 people nationwide and has been named Canadian Mortgage Lender of the Year by the Canadian Lending Association in both 2023 and 2024.

items.description: Two new surveys suggest that Quebecers and Canadians are concerned about the economic situation, inflation, and the impact of the trade war with the United States as the holidays approach.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Sports Experts employee walks past a sign advertising Black Friday sales in Montreal on Friday, Nov. 29, 2024. (THE CANADIAN PRESS/Christinne Muschi)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Christinne Muschi</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Two new surveys suggest that Quebecers and Canadians are concerned about the economic situation, inflation, and the impact of the trade war with the United States as the holidays approach.
items.body:
Two new surveys suggest that Quebecers and Canadians are concerned about the economic situation, inflation, and the impact of the trade war with the United States as the holidays approach.

Data from both the Retail Council of Quebec and a Canada-wide poll also show that consumers intend to buy Canadian or Quebec products.

The surveys, which have different questions and methodologies, give slightly different results when it comes to spending expectations.

Data from the Retail Council of Quebec’s (CQCD) quarterly barometer shows that Quebecers expect their holiday spending to increase by about five per cent.

But the survey also reveals that sales of electronics and computer equipment, furniture, appliances, and alcohol are expected to decline.

However, a Canada-wide Angus Reid poll conducted by the credit firm Money Mart reveals that nearly 80 per cent of respondents expect inflation to weigh heavily on their holiday spending, and that nearly six in 10 plan to spend less than in 2025. That figure rises for households with an income below $50,000.

The head of the Retail Council of Quebec is encouraging consumers to follow through on their intentions to buy local, while warning about the lure of budget platforms such as TEMU and SHEIN.

In his view, the low-end products sold by these platforms benefit consumers in the short term, but don’t last in the medium term and destroy local businesses.

“With the growing poverty of the population in Quebec and Canada, along with inflation and rising interest rates, people are unfortunately being pushed to buy much larger quantities through these networks,” Damien Silès said.

Such platforms, he added, don’t follow laws, are an “environmental disaster” and “operate through plagiarism.”

The two surveys also reinforce the popularity of end-of-year sales for both Canadian and Quebec consumers.

The CQCD Barometer highlights that nearly six in 10 Quebecers intend to do their shopping starting during the Black Friday period — a proportion that has risen by 17 per cent over the past five years.

Many of these sales are already underway, even though the real Black Friday isn’t until Nov. 27.

These sales, which mark the start of the Christmas shopping season, are important to stores, often accounting for 30 to 50 per cent of revenue.

“So, it’s a very, very important time of year,” Silès says.

The Money Mart survey suggests households are getting more anxious about managing seasonal spending.

Last year, 18 per cent of respondents expected to have a harder time coping with holiday expenses than the previous year, which has now risen to 26 per cent.

Less than half of holiday shoppers will dip into their savings, but 55 per cent will buy on credit, the survey shows.

It also found that 22 per cent of Canadians with children living at home are still paying off debts incurred during the 2025 holiday season.

In addition, one-third of respondents would struggle to cover an unexpected expense during the holiday season.

The Money Mart survey was conducted online by Angus Reid from Sept. 22 to 24 among 1,503 Canadian adults.

The CQCD Barometer, meanwhile, is based on an online survey by ORAMA Marketing, conducted among 1,013 respondents from Oct. 6 to 21.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes survey standards, believes it is impossible to assign a margin of error to online surveys because they do not constitute a random sample of the population.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

items.body:
Opening Statement before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance

Stephen Punwasi, Co-Founder and Chief Data Analyst, Better Dwelling.

Ottawa, November 19, 2026.

As prepared for delivery.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and members of the committee.

My name’s Stephen Punwasi, and my background is in behavioural finance and the levers that drive asset prices. I’m also the co-founder of Better Dwelling, Canada’s largest independent housing news outlet, where we focus on reducing information asymmetry.

Information asymmetry occurs when one party is better informed about a transaction than the other. This slants the odds in their favour, helping them to win. Since there’s no shortage of people willing to sing the praises—or fear mongering—over government spending, I’m going to do what we do at Better Dwelling and just explain the market dynamics and risk, hoping it reduces the asymmetry for all parties.

So let’s talk about borrowing, debt, and risks.

There are three things households and policymakers should understand about credit markets.

One: debt is future income, spent today, plus interest.

Borrowing for productive uses can pay for itself. The public is generally in agreement here, and the language Ottawa’s using resonates with that sentiment. However, an investment has to produce a return after its costs, including interest and opportunity costs.

Right now, Ottawa can’t tell us where the money is going. Roughly $260 billion is going to Crown Corporation loans and equity, and the budget doesn’t break down which ones get what. Housing is a good example. The PBO previously said it was unclear if the spending helped or just took credit for things that were happening. Since then, Ottawa ramped up the spending, building costs dropped, and fewer homes are being built. It costs less to build a home, the subsidies have climbed, and fewer are being built. That makes it pretty clear.

The bank grills me if I want to take my own money out for a used car. $260 billion is the equivalent of 16 million Canadian households going to work and paying taxes for a year, but Ottawa won’t tell the public where it’s going?

Two: The Price of Debt Depends On Who’s Borrowing

Debt is priced by supply, demand and risk. Ottawa borrows at the lowest rates in the country, since it runs the printing press. The issue is what happens next. Through its Crown corporations, it passes that cheap credit on to the projects it chooses.

Everyone outside those programs borrows at market rates. Small businesses can’t issue bonds, neither can households. They have to borrow from banks, and according to the latest lending conditions survey, face tighter conditions. Ottawa isn’t just borrowing, it’s helping big businesses succeed, while slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canada’s workers. That’s a subsidy, and like any corporate handout, the public should know what it’s paying for.

Three: Know Your Lender & How Long They’ll Stay

Policymakers have been boasting of the foreign investment made in Canada, but they’ve been light on the details. Let me help with that. Almost zero of the net investment has been in equities. It’s all debt. Foreign investors absorbed all of Ottawa’s net new issuance in the first half of this year. This has created a tail risk that threatens the whole financial system, and I’m not just being hyperbolic. The Bank of Canada has quietly confirmed it.

Hedge funds account for over 40 percent of purchases at auctions, and typically fund those positions with overnight or short-term borrowing. They aren’t lenders the way a household thinks of one. They’re renting the bonds, on borrowed money, a day at a time.

The Bank of Canada warns that a funding disruption could force them to sell suddenly, calling it a “self-reinforcing liquidity spiral.” If I were advising a hedge fund today, I would tell them to make that play too.

During the last crisis, fiscal dominance forced the BoC to buy government bonds to provide liquidity. It was a big payday for investors; the BoC ended up with a $10 billion loss, the equivalent of 625,000 households’ federal taxes for a year.

It will happen again. A crisis for Canadians is a massive win for these foreign investors. Make no mistake, this play is a bet against Canada, not for it. This will be the difference between a recession and a financial crisis.

That backstop keeps Ottawa’s borrowing cheap today. The risk doesn’t go away. It moves to the public.

Is Ottawa making responsible investments for the future of Canada? I don’t know, and anyone who definitively says it is or isn’t is lying. Because Ottawa isn’t sure where the money is going either, it’s like the funds are allocated before anything is actually planned.

I’d ask the committee for three things. First, asset-level reporting for Crown lending and equity, including the subsidy built into below-market loans, so Parliament can see where the spending goes—and the public knows what their kids will be paying for. Second, outcome reporting for conditional transfers like housing. It’s simply not enough to spend money and take credit for wins and blame the economy for the losses. Third, reporting on who holds federal debt, how concentrated that base is, and how much of it is funded with short-term leverage, alongside each budget.

Banks and investors would ask those questions. Parliament—and the public—should be able to ask Ottawa them.

Thank you. I’m happy to take your questions.

items._ogDesc: The approved project comprises a 24-storey concrete tower and 2-storey townhouse and an amenity building
items.body:
A partially-built residential high-rise building in Surrey’s City Centre, that is under a court-ordered sale, is back on the market.

Appearing to have found a buyer as it was listed this summer as being under contract, the project in the 13000-block of 101 Avenue is once again available, listed at $30 million.

“Construction on the project has progressed to the sixth floor above grade. Buyers can restart construction and benefit from over $23 million in hard costs spent to date, along with fully paid for entitlements and completed design drawings,” the listing notes.

It had been marketed as “Centra,”an approved project comprising a 24-storey concrete tower and a two-storey townhouse and amenity building.

The project has 167 residential units above 194 stalls in two levels of underground parking.

The listing also notes, “Prior to construction delays, the project was successfully pre-sold; however, all contracts have since been rescinded, offering a new owner a clean slate to relaunch a sales program or reposition the asset as a market rental.”

Construction on the project ceased in August 2024 and Alvarez & Marsal Canada Inc. was appointed the receiver and manager earlier this year.

Home sales forecast to move up in Greater Vancouver next year

A new report by the British Columbia Real Estate Association (BCREA) forecasts home sales in Greater Vancouver going up, however, prices won’t correspond to that level of increase.

The BCREA’s 2026 Fourth Quarter Housing Forecast notes Multiple Listing Service (MLS) residential sales in BC are forecast to fall 4.5 per cent to 67,025 units this year.

The report notes that with active listings near their highest level since 2015, and additional pressure from elevated new-home inventory, the BCREA anticipates the average price in B.C. will fall by 1.2 per cent in 2026.

That decrease largely reflects disproportionate weakness in more expensive markets in the Lower Mainland, casting downward pressure on the broader provincial average price, the report explains.

In 2027, MLS residential sales are forecast to move higher, rising 7.2 per cent to 71,840 units.

Greater Vancouver is forecast to see an 8.7 per cent increase in 2027, after seeing decreases the previous two years.

The Fraser Valley is forecast to see an increase of 9.1 per cent.

The 2027 average MLS price is forecast to go up 2.2 per cent in Greater Vancouver and 1.8 per cent in the Fraser Valley.

“British Columbia’s housing market continues to face a challenging economic environment, as mounting headwinds fuel hesitancy among prospective buyers,” said BCREA Chief Economist Brendon Ogmundson in a news release. “Ultimately, we expect a modest recovery in home sales in 2027 as the impacts of new United States tariffs fade and fixed mortgage rates decline.”

items.title: Tracking Toronto’s 5 Tallest Rental, Condo Proposals (So Far) This Fall
items.description:
Toronto has never been shy about building up, and newsy developments like the Pinnacle towers and One Bloor West are proof that the high-rise fixation is alive and well.

But it’s not just the 80-storey-plus cohort that’s worth paying attention to. If you sift through the steady stream of development applications hitting the City’s desk, proposals in the the 40- to 60-storey range are impressive in their own rights, promising to add hundreds of new homes to the city while reshaping neighbourhood skylines.

Since September, there have been a handful of proposals that fit that bill, including a 56-storey rental that would displace the century-old City Morgue, a pair of 46-storey condos that have come out the other side of receivership, and a 61-storey condo slated for the burgeoning Etobicoke City Centre area. Here’s what's planned.

56 Storeys: 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E

Rendering of 86 and 100-108 Lombard St and 103 Richmond St E/WZMH Architects

After initially proposing a 59-storey mixed-use building in 2022, Forum Asset Management and Slate Asset Management secured OLT approvals in 2025 for a much taller, 72-storey tower at 86 and 100-108 Lombard Street and 103 Richmond Street East — a parcel in Toronto’s Old Town area.

The most recent version of the proposal is considerably scaled back, describing a 56-storey mixed-use building (exclusive of a two-storey mechanical penthouse). The other major way the development departs from past plans is the unit tenure; while the 2022 proposal asked for 480 condo units, and the 2025 settlement was for 702 condo units, Forum and Slate are now planning 523 purpose-built rental units, alongside space for office and retail. The heritage-designated former City Morgue building at 86 Lombard Street would be relocated to the eastern portion of the development site to make way for the proposed.

Learn more.

50 Storeys & 50 Storeys: 60 Overlea Blvd

Rendering of 60 Overlea Blvd/Sweeny&Co Architects

The Ontario Line is inching towards the finish line, and 60 Overlea Boulevard in Thorncliffe Park — currently occupied by an under-utilized retail plaza — is one of the many Toronto addresses that will benefit from the forthcoming transit connectivity. The site is less than 500 metres from the future Thorncliffe Park station, and a proposal from landowner Plazaworks Inc. describes a pair of 50-storey towers with a shared podium. All 1,261 units would be rental in tenure, while the ground floor would be reserved for non-residential uses, including a potential childcare facility.

Plazaworks is also seeking official plan and zoning bylaw amendments to re-designate the property from General Employment Areas to Mixed Use Areas, which would pave the way for some of the proposed non-residential space to be used for “employment-generating uses.”

Learn more.

46 Storeys & 46 Storeys: 7 Labatt Ave And 77 River St

Rendering of 7 Labatt Ave and 77 River St/Giannone Petricone Associates

A long-stalled development site at 7 Labatt Avenue and 77 River Street — on the edge of Regent Park, about a kilometre from the future Corktown station of the Ontario Line — is now under the ownership of KingSett Capital, with the firm now planning a pair of 46-storey towers. The high-rises would have 1,170 condo units between them, while a separate two-storey Salvation Army building is planned to the east (replacing the Salvation Army building currently at 7 Labatt). The plans also include a publicly accessible open space running between the 46-storey towers.

The site was initially being redeveloped by TAS in favour of their “Labatt Village” project, set to include 48- and 44-storey buildings with 1,240 units. The project was placed under receivership in February, and KingSett took over through an $84.15-million credit bid this summer, paving the way for the site’s next chapter.

Learn more.

50 Storeys: 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave

Rendering of 4632-4648 Yonge St and 16-18 Cameron Ave/Arcadis

While some developments hinge on the forthcoming Ontario Line, others make use of the transit Toronto already has. A proposal from Yonge and Cameron LP is for a 50-storey mixed-use tower at 4632–4648 Yonge Street and 16–18 Cameron Avenue in North York, where it would replace a two-storey commercial plaza and two detached houses around 200 metres from the Sheppard-Yonge subway station. The site is also within the North York Centre and a designated Protected Major Transit Station Area, where the City is encouraging further intensification.

The development would introduce 569 new residential units to the site — all condo in tenure — and the continued operation of the existing autobody shop at 4656 Yonge. The tower would also include ground-floor retail and indoor and outdoor amenity spaces designed with families with children and pet owners in mind.

Learn more.

61 Storeys: 1234 Islington Ave

Rendering of 1234 Islington Ave/Sweeny&Co Architects

After securing City Council approvals in June, Montez Corporation has moved ahead with site plan control application for a 61-storey mixed-use tower at 1243 Islington Avenue in central Etobicoke, where it would replace a 12-storey office building. Though the City approved 702 condo units and a retail component for the site, the latest planning documents show that the unit-count has been cut down to 527. In addition, it seems the project has been switched to purpose-built rental, and 16 units are planned to be affordable.

The site is less than 200 metres from Islington Station, within a Protected Major Transit Station Area, and leans into a wider push to reshape the neighbourhood into a more complete community. Nearby, the new Etobicoke Civic Centre is coming up on what’s locally known as the Westwood Theatre Lands, where it will accommodate a new library, recreation centre, child-care centre, public health clinic, and civic square.

items.title: OSFI cuts capital rules for small banks to boost mortgage competition
items.description: Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes
items.content: <p>Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307089600249717.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Smaller lenders gain room to compete for mortgage clients under OSFI’s latest capital changes
items.body:
Canada’s banking regulator moved to ease capital constraints on the country’s smaller lenders, launching a Competitive Prudential Initiative designed to narrow the structural gap between smaller institutions and the dominant Big Six in key lending markets, including residential mortgages.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) announced the initiative as the centrepiece of its fourth Quarterly Release of 2026.

The changes target small and medium-sized banks (SMSBs) and federal credit unions, reducing risk-weighted assets — the measure determining how much capital a lender must hold against potential loan losses — across residential mortgages, small and medium-sized business lending, and corporate lending.

Under the proposals, the risk weight for loans to small and medium-sized businesses would fall to 65% from 75%, while corporate lending risk weights would drop to 80% from 100%.

OSFI will also reduce capital requirements for residential mortgages with credit bureau scores above 720.

Levelling the playing field

The move addresses a structural imbalance that has long given Canada’s domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) a capital advantage over their smaller rivals.

Peter Routledge, Superintendent of Financial Institutions at OSFI, called it “our most ambitious effort to date to level the playing field in Canadian banking without materially impacting the resilience of the system,” adding that the initiative was about “giving smaller deposit-takers greater room for prudent risk-taking.”

The changes align with Budget 2026, which proposes amending the OSFI Act to introduce a secondary competition mandate, formally requiring the regulator to weigh competitive balance alongside financial stability.

Ottawa has proposed Bank Act amendments to widen banking competition, with broader measures directly targeting the Big Six’s hold on the sector.

What it means for brokers

For mortgage brokers, a wider field of better-capitalised smaller lenders could translate into greater product diversity and more competitive rate options for clients.

Brokers command a 33% share of the Canadian mortgage market, up four percentage points since 2022, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s 2024 Mid-Year Report.

Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Canada, has described the broader direction of competition reform as “exactly the kind of structural signal that tells fintech innovators, consumers and incumbents: this market is open for business.”

He added that “when more institutions enter the market, Canadians gain better rates and innovative options,” and stressed the need for follow-through: “This is a meaningful step forward, but now we must ensure the entire ecosystem evolves in tandem.”

The initiative builds on OSFI’s June decision to lower the Domestic Stability Buffer, releasing an estimated $74 billion in excess capital from Canada’s six largest banks.

Proposed changes are open for public consultation until February 17, 2027, with final guidelines expected in late 2027 or early 2028.

items.title: Scotiabank home financing adviser class action certified in Ontario
items.description: Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims
items.content: <p>Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307048260813539.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ontario court certifies Scotiabank class action over unpaid vacation and holiday pay claims
items.body:
An Ontario court has certified a class action lawsuit against The Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotiabank) alleging the lender failed to pay vacation pay and statutory holiday pay owed to thousands of current and former home financing advisers (HFAs) under the Canada Labour Code (CLC).

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice certified the case — Deacon v. Bank of Nova Scotia, 2026 ONSC 1793 — on March 31.

The representative plaintiffs are Nathalie Deacon, a current Scotiabank HFA, and Gail Ouellette, a retired HFA, both represented by Paliare Roland Rosenberg Rothstein LLP, a Toronto-based litigation firm.

Scotiabank denies all allegations, and no claims have been proven in court.

What the class action alleges

The suit contends that Scotiabank, one of Canada’s Big Six banks with approximately $1.5 trillion in assets as at April 30, excluded variable pay components when calculating vacation and statutory holiday pay entitlements for its HFAs — a commission-based role within its real estate secured lending division.

For retired class members, the plaintiffs further allege the bank failed to calculate pension entitlements based on total compensation.

The class covers all HFAs, including those previously carrying the title of Mortgage Development Manager, employed between November 1, 2009, and March 31, 2026.

The Ontario Class Proceedings Fund provided financial backing for the case and would receive 10% of any recovery if the action succeeds.

The timing places the certification within a period of considerable internal change at Scotiabank. The bank eliminated approximately 3,000 roles through its late-2025 restructuring, drawing sustained scrutiny to its employment practices.

That same period also saw new senior appointments to its real estate secured lending and risk units in November 2025, as the bank pushed to accelerate its broader transformation strategy.

Scotiabank reported net income of $2.95 billion for the three months ended July 31, the strongest quarter in its history.

The certification adds to pressure on federally regulated lenders over how commission-based staff compensation is structured. 

Compensation is one of the three factors mortgage professionals consistently rank highest when choosing where to work.

“The strongest organizations invest in their people through mentorship, coaching, and real career development rather than simply focusing on production. They understand that mortgage professionals are running businesses within a business,” Michelle Campbell, mortgage broker at MA – A Better Way Mortgage Group, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in March.

“Professionals also want growth opportunities, which could be mentorship roles, leadership pathways, specialization in certain lending areas, or business coaching.”

items.title: Toronto commercial real estate investment already outpaces 2025
items.description: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.content: <p>Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307039780020741.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Big-ticket deals return as office and multifamily drive a commercial rebound brokers can’t ignore
items.body:
Toronto commercial real estate investment has already surpassed its full-year 2025 total. Nearly $13.5 billion in transactions closed across the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) in the first nine months of 2026, according to Avison Young’s Greater Toronto investment review for the third quarter. That total is up 55% from the same period last year.

Third-quarter volume reached $4.4 billion, a 52% gain from Q3 2025, though 22% below a stronger second quarter. The number of trades rose a more modest 16% year to date, to 1,356.

“The much larger rise in dollar volume versus number of transactions is indicative of the increasing occurrence of large deals in the market,” the report said.

Multifamily leads as office capital returns

Multifamily was the quarter’s largest asset class at just over $1.7 billion, or 39% of total volume, up 310% year over year. Welltower Inc.’s $414 million purchase of a seniors’ housing portfolio from Amica Senior Lifestyles anchored the quarter.

Office posted the sharpest turnaround, with investment up 278% to $777 million. The largest deal was GWL Realty Advisors’ $243.6 million acquisition of 123 Front St. W. in Toronto from Oxford Properties. GTA-wide office availability fell 190 basis points from a year earlier to 17.6%.

“The improvements in the leasing market have allowed lenders to approach office assets with less apprehension (although this is still submarket- and asset-specific),” the report said.

“With tenant demand rising and little to no new supply in the development pipeline across downtown and suburban markets, investors’ view of the value of existing assets is increasing.”

Damon Conrad, vice-president at REMAX Canada Commercial, flagged the quality divide when investors flooding back to Toronto’s office sector first made headlines this year.

“I think office is seeing clear separation between premium amenity-rich buildings and the older assets that need repositioning,” Conrad told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

Industrial was the laggard. Volume fell 22% to $1.2 billion, and for the first time since Q3 2023, it was not the GTA’s most-traded asset class.

Rate hike tests lender appetite

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on Oct. 28, its first increase since July 2023. Avison Young warned that higher borrowing costs could affect how investors view asset values.

“With signs that both Canada and the US may continue to raise interest rates to combat inflation, there is the possibility that higher borrowing costs could impact investors’ views on asset values and demand for commercial real estate,” the report said.

The average multifamily capitalization rate, the ratio of a property’s net operating income to its sale price, rose 15 basis points to 4.09%.

“Nevertheless, traditional banks and funding sources are still actively seeking lending opportunities, and the situation surrounding tariffs and petroleum supply continues to evolve – with knock-on effects for the Canadian economy and real estate markets,” the report said.

Richard Joy, executive director at the Urban Land Institute in Toronto, has described an uneven recovery, a theme behind equity shortages threatening Canadian commercial refinancing in 2027.

“The GTA’s real estate market is moving at different speeds. Industrial and premium office show signs of recovery, while condominiums remain challenged,” Joy said.

“Investors remain cautious yet generally optimistic heading into the final months of the year,” the report said.

Avison Young expects strong activity in the fourth quarter.
